newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma City anxious for McVeigh trial to begin.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma City anxious for McVeigh trial to begin.

text.p: The trial of Oklahoma City bombing defendant Timothy McVeigh cannot come a minute too soon for the people who lived through the tragedy that changed forever this heartland city.

News Friday that U.S. District Judge Richard Matsch, sitting in Denver, set a trial date of March 31 for McVeigh brought both relief and impatience for officials, survivors and family members of the 168 people who died in the April 19, 1995, bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building.
"The sooner the better," Oklahoma City Mayor Ron Norick said. "There's a lot of families around here that have been put off and put off and put off. It's time this thing moves forward."
He said that by the time the trial gets underway, it will have been almost two years since the bombing. "I think that's way too long. We're supposed to have a speedy justice system," Norick said.
McVeigh will be tried separately from his former army buddy Terry Nichols, whose trial date has not yet been set.
The trial was moved to Denver because of publicity in Oklahoma following the bombing.
Prosecutors say the two detonated a 4,800-pound fertiliser bomb in Oklahoma City because of their hatred for the federal government. Both men have pleaded not guilty.
The blast destroyed the Murrah building and damaged 300 other buildings in the city. Along with the dead, 850 people were injured.

Kathleen Treanor, whose 4-year-old daughter was killed in the blast, said she was glad the trial date had been set. She accused McVeigh's defence attorneys of delaying the proceedings in hopes that memories would fade and their client would have a better chance of acquittal.
"I'm sure that's why the defence for the accused is trying to drag it out. But no one's going to forget this," she said.
"We're still dealing with this thing on a daily basis," Treanor said. "There's no normal anymore."
Martin Cash, who worked in the Murrah building but survived the blast, said he was anxious for the trial to begin.
The irony, Cash said, is that he worked for 22 years in the Veterans Administration "just trying to help guys likes McVeigh and Nichols."
"My main purpose is to see that justice is done against these guys who tried to kill me," said Cash, who lost his left eye in the bombing and has a titantium plate in his skull.
Norick said the trial would be another step in Oklahoma City's healing process. "The trial will be the beginning of the end, but there's still a a long way to go," he said.
